turns.prompt_text: I need to source sheets of metal for a lot of my projects, primarily in making the telescoping covers of beehives The other use is for the beehive frame incubator system that uses sunlight to trap heat in a box My understanding is that it requires the ultraviolet light to get trapped in the box and turn itself into heat when it makes contact with materials within the box The wood with black spray paint works but metal I imagine would be a whole lot better But I don't understand is why I cannot use aluminum foil Besides for it tearing if I were very delicate with it and it did not tear, why would the other downsides be? Is the thickness of really that important? And can that not be sold by using quite a few layers?
turns.response_html:
Building your own structural hives and custom incubators is a great way to prototype exactly what you need. But when it comes to trapping heat, there are a few physics principles to clear up regarding how light and metal interact.

The Physics of Your Solar Incubator

First, it is actually not the ultraviolet (UV) light doing the heavy lifting—it is primarily visible light and short-wave infrared radiation.

The glass or plastic on your incubator lets that solar radiation in. When it hits a dark, absorptive surface, it turns into long-wave thermal energy (heat). That long-wave heat cannot pass back through the glass, so it gets trapped. This is the classic greenhouse effect.

Your wood with black spray paint works well because the dark matte color absorbs the radiation. Bare metal, however, is highly reflective. If you use bare metal, it will bounce the sunlight right back out. To make metal outperform your black-painted wood, you must paint the metal flat black. Once painted, the metal will conduct that heat evenly across the whole surface, eliminating cold spots.

Why Aluminum Foil Fails (Besides Tearing)

If you use aluminum foil, you run into two major physics problems:

  1. High Reflectivity (Albedo): Bare aluminum foil is essentially a mirror. It reflects about 90% of solar radiation instead of absorbing it.
  2. Zero Thermal Mass: Thickness is incredibly important. A material needs mass to store heat. Because foil is paper-thin, it has virtually zero thermal mass. It might get hot instantly, but the second a cloud passes over, it loses all its heat. A thicker sheet of metal (like 22-gauge steel or aluminum) absorbs the heat and radiates it steadily, keeping the internal temperature of your incubator stable.

turns.prompt_text: I have some metal from some microwaves come to think of it. I imagine if I bend it around the bottom of the box, I could make a base. Then spray it black of course. If I can, should I also cover the sides with black spray painted metal? Is the more metal the better? Could I just toss some rebar in there? Could I line the sides with something like copper coils? Would that help?
turns.response_html:
Repurposing microwave casing is a great DIY move. The steel is sturdy, has decent thickness, and is practically free.

Bending it to form a base pan and spraying it flat black is exactly the right approach. When the sun hits it, it will heat up nicely. But to get this incubator running at peak efficiency, you have to balance heat absorption with heat retention.

Here is how those other materials play into that balance:

Should you cover the sides with black metal?

Only if the sun actually hits them.

Black metal only absorbs heat when exposed to direct light. If the sides of your incubator are in the shadow of the frame or the box itself, black metal on the sides won't pull in any new solar energy.

Worse, if you just line the sides with metal without heavily insulating the outside of the box, that metal will act as a thermal bridge. It will conduct the heat from your base pan straight to the outside air. For the sides, you are usually better off focusing on insulation (like foam board or thick wood) to keep the heat trapped in the air space, rather than adding metal just for the sake of it.

Is more metal better? (The Rebar Question)

Yes and no. Adding more metal (like tossing in rebar) increases your thermal mass.

Think of thermal mass like a battery for heat:

  • The Pros: If you have a lot of metal, it stores a massive amount of heat. Once it gets hot, it stays hot for a long time. If a cloud passes over for 20 minutes, your incubator's temperature won't plummet.
  • The Cons: It takes significantly more energy (and time) to "charge" that battery. If you throw thick rebar into the box, the sun has to heat up all of that steel before the air in the box gets hot.

If you are using this as a wax melter where you need to hit peak temperatures (around 150°F / 65°C) quickly on a partly cloudy day, too much mass will prevent the box from ever getting hot enough. The microwave base alone is probably the perfect sweet spot of absorbing heat quickly and holding it steadily.

turns.prompt_text: What if there were solar panels on the side of the box connected to copper wires acting as resistors?
turns.response_html:
That is a clever idea—you are basically describing how an electric space heater works, just powered by a solar panel. While it absolutely works in theory, physics makes this a massive downgrade in efficiency compared to what you are already doing.

There are two major roadblocks to this setup: the physics of energy conversion and the electrical properties of copper.

The Efficiency Problem

Every time you convert energy from one form to another, you lose some of it.

  • Your current passive setup (Solar Thermal): Sunlight passes through glass, hits black metal, and turns directly into heat. A well-designed passive solar box can capture 60% to 80% of the sun's energy that hits it.
  • The solar panel setup (Photovoltaic): Standard solar panels are only about 15% to 22% efficient at turning sunlight into electricity. Even though a resistor is 100% efficient at turning that electricity into heat, your bottleneck is the panel.

turns.prompt_text: Is there anything I can do to make this work better? What I'm magnifying glass like a really large one. What about insulation? I imagine this thing has to be sealed
turns.response_html:
Using a magnifying glass sounds like a great way to supercharge the heat, but for an incubator or wax melter, it will actually ruin your project—and possibly start a fire.

Here is why, along with how to properly trap the heat using insulation and sealing.

The Magnifying Glass Problem

A magnifying glass (or a large Fresnel lens, like the ones pulled from old projection TVs) takes all the sunlight hitting a large area and concentrates it into a tiny focal point.

  • The problem: You need ambient, distributed heat to melt wax or keep an incubator warm (usually around 140°F to 180°F). A magnifying glass creates localized, extreme heat (often exceeding 1,000°F).
  • The result: Instead of gently heating your box, the focal point will scorch your wax, burn a hole straight through your black-painted microwave metal, and ignite the wooden base underneath it.

You want the flat glass you are already using. It distributes the solar radiation evenly across the entire black metal pan.

Why Sealing and Insulation are Mandatory

You are spot-on about sealing it. A solar box works exactly like a car parked in the sun with the windows rolled up. If you crack a window even half an inch, the heat escapes almost instantly.

If your box is just bare wood and glass with gaps, it will fight a losing battle against the outside air temperature.

turns.prompt_text: Sealing will be the toughest part Because on the bottom I have a few more bottom layers with sieves And in order to make them airtight I could just duct tape them Same with the top. I have two panes of glass from picture frames And I could just duct tape them But I will need some other liquid adhesive or such to ensure there are no gaps
turns.response_html:
The layered sieve design is brilliant for melting and filtering all in one go, but you definitely have a few different sealing problems to tackle here.

Whatever you do, skip the standard duct tape.

Duct tape uses a rubber-based adhesive that completely breaks down and turns to gooey sludge right around 140°F (60°C). A solar wax melter will easily hit 180°F (82°C) or higher. Within a week, the tape will slide right off, leaving a sticky residue everywhere and ruining your seal.

Here is exactly what you should use for the different parts of your box:

1. Sealing the Glass (The Permanent Seal)

For the liquid adhesive holding your picture frame glass to the top layer of the box, the absolute best choice is 100% silicone sealant.

If you happen to have any leftover aquarium-safe silicone sitting around from setting up your 20-gallon tank, that is actually the perfect material to use here. It is built entirely for glass-to-glass and glass-to-wood bonds, easily handles temperatures over 300°F (150°C), and most importantly, it won't off-gas toxic chemicals into your wax once it cures.

A warning on picture frame glass: It is extremely thin and not tempered. When the wood of your box heats up in the sun, it will warp and expand. If you use a rigid glue (like wood glue, epoxy, or superglue), the expanding wood will torque the glass and shatter it instantly. Silicone stays rubbery and acts as a shock absorber, letting the wood and glass expand at different rates without breaking.

2. Sealing the Sieve Layers (The Removable Seal)

Because you have multiple sieve layers, you need a way to seal them while they are stacked, but you also need to take them apart to harvest the wax and clean the filters.

Instead of taping them every time, line the mating edges of each layer with high-temperature silicone weatherstripping (often sold as "smoker gasket" or "oven gasket"). When you stack the sieve layers on top of each other, the weight of the box will compress the gasket, giving you an airtight seal that you can just lift apart whenever you want.

3. If You Must Tape

If you find that your sieve layers don't sit perfectly flat against the gaskets and you have to tape the outside seams to stop air leaks, use HVAC Aluminum Foil Tape.

This is the shiny, metallic tape used on heating ducts. Its adhesive is specifically engineered to handle high heat without melting, and the foil backing will reflect the sun rather than baking into a sludge.

turns.prompt_text: Okay now I want to think about the glass. The top I have some. I believe they are acrylic and not class frames because when I look through them there is some matte finish going on so everything's a little blurred underneath And I'm pretty sure I want to use glass and not acrylic or anything else
turns.response_html:
You are absolutely right to trust your instinct here. You want to ditch the acrylic and use real glass for this project.

But before you toss those panels out, check the corners. A lot of new acrylic picture frames come with a tightly adhered, frosted protective film on both sides that makes everything look blurry and matte. If you scratch the very corner, you might find you can peel it off to reveal clear plastic.

Even if it does peel perfectly clear, though, you still do not want it for a solar wax melter.

Why Glass Beats Acrylic for Solar Heating

Your instinct to avoid plastic is backed directly by the thermodynamics of what you are building:

  1. The Melting Point: A good solar box on a sunny summer day will easily clear 180°F (82°C). Standard extruded acrylic starts to soften, warp, and sag at around 160°F (71°C). If you use acrylic for the lid, it will eventually bow inward and could collapse into your wax. Glass will not warp or sag, no matter how hot the box gets.
  2. The Greenhouse Trap: Glass is specifically excellent at creating the greenhouse effect. It allows short-wave solar radiation (sunlight) to pass through easily, but it is highly opaque to long-wave infrared radiation (the heat radiating off your black metal pan). Acrylic lets a bit more of that long-wave heat escape back out into the atmosphere.
  3. UV Degradation: Constant exposure to direct sunlight causes standard acrylic to yellow, become brittle, and turn cloudy (crazing) over time. This cloudiness blocks sunlight and ruins the efficiency of the melter. Glass will stay crystal clear for decades.

What Kind of Glass to Look For

Since picture frame glass is very thin, it is highly susceptible to thermal shock—if a cold rain hits the hot glass, it will shatter instantly. It is also fragile if you accidentally drop a tool on it.

If you have access to scrap materials from construction or demolition sites, keep an eye out for tempered glass. The glass from an old oven door, a discarded microwave door, or a broken sliding glass patio door is ideal. It is thick, handles extreme temperature swings without breaking, and traps heat incredibly well.

If you are stuck with picture frame glass for now, it will definitely work to get your prototype up and running—just handle it carefully and try to keep it out of sudden rainstorms while it is hot.

turns.prompt_text: Yes, I'm going to have to run with this acrylic for now I imagine buying tempered glass would be somewhat expensive I wonder if there are any other alternatives I could go with?
turns.response_html:
Running with the acrylic for the prototype is a smart move. It will let you test your dimensions, sieve layers, and seals before you invest anything more into it. If it sags a little bit in the meantime, it's not the end of the world for a proof-of-concept.

When you are ready to upgrade, you absolutely do not need to buy brand-new custom tempered glass. There are two great alternatives that will save you money while giving you the heat resistance you need.

1. Intercepting Construction Scrap (Free)

Before spending any money, take a look around the staging ground or workshop garage at your dad's construction company.

Renovation and demolition jobs constantly throw out old residential double-pane windows, sliding glass patio doors, or scrap tempered glass. A discarded double-pane window sash is basically a pre-built, perfectly sealed, highly insulated lid ready to be dropped onto a solar melter.

If there isn't anything immediately available in the yard, checking the local Habitat for Humanity ReStore (there is one right down the road in Ames or nearby in Des Moines) is your next best bet. You can usually pick up a heavy-duty, tempered double-pane window for under $20.

2. Twin-Wall Polycarbonate

If you want to stick with plastic because it is lighter and easier to cut, you want polycarbonate, not acrylic.

turns.prompt_text: Where can I find this? Double-sided polycarbonate
turns.response_html:
You can easily grab twin-wall polycarbonate right off the shelf at a few of the local hardware stores around Ames today.

The Sunlite Polycarbonate Panel sheet is a lightweight but rugged twin-wall insulated material that easily handles high temperatures and is perfect for trapping solar heat.

Here are the best places to look locally:

  • Menards: They typically stock large 6mm twin-wall panels right in the outdoor, roofing, or greenhouse sections. You can buy a single large sheet and easily cut it down to fit multiple box lids.
  • Home Depot: They carry a few variations of clear multi-wall polycarbonate (like the Sunlite brand) in the roofing materials aisle.

When you go to pick up a sheet, be sure to also grab some solid aluminum or foil tape. Because the material is fluted with air channels running through the middle, any dirt, sawdust, or moisture that gets inside those channels will ruin your insulation and clarity. You have to seal the cut edges immediately.

turns.prompt_text: Now let's think about the adhesive used to seal the box I think using silicone might work if I put silicone on every interface between two sections, and then this keeps it modular so that I can place the sections together. But then I will require using some pressure, some weight on top of the box to really press the seal closed between each layer Right now there is the top layer which holds the class. There's the box which holds the frames and there are two layers of sieves and then there's a bottom metal board
turns.response_html:
A five-layer modular stack (lid, frames box, two sieves, metal base) is a fantastic design for processing, but you have correctly identified the main flaw: liquid silicone is a permanent glue. If you apply it wet to every interface and stack them, you won't have a modular box—you'll have one solid, permanently glued block of wood.

If you let the silicone dry before stacking them, the cured silicone is too firm and slick to compress properly under normal weight, leaving you with tiny air gaps.

You have two good options here: casting a custom gasket, or using a mechanical clamp.

Option 1: The "Form-in-Place" Silicone Gasket

If you want to use the silicone you already have, you can cast custom, perfectly mated rubber gaskets directly onto the wood without gluing the boxes together. You just need a release agent.

Option 2: Mechanical Clamping (Instead of Dead Weight)

Using dead weight (like a cinderblock or a bucket of water) on top of the stack is the traditional way to compress seals. However, a five-layer stack is tall. Putting heavy weight on the very top makes it prone to tipping, and puts a lot of bowing pressure directly on your acrylic lid.

Instead of relying on gravity, you could fire up the Bambu A1 and run off a few sets of over-center toggle latches.

Printing functional hardware out of PETG or ABS (PLA will warp in the sun) would allow you to physically snap the sieve layers and frames box down tight against each other. This mechanically locks the compression in place across all the layers without putting any dangerous pressure on your lid.

turns.prompt_text: Okay back to the last. What a glass from like an aquarium work like a fish tank
turns.response_html:
If you are thinking about breaking down an old 20-gallon tank or picking up a cheap used one, that glass is actually a massive upgrade over both the acrylic and the picture frames—but it comes with one major risk.

The Good: Thickness and Clarity

Aquarium glass is significantly thicker than picture frame glass (usually between 1/8" and 1/4" thick for smaller tanks). This thickness gives it a much higher thermal mass, meaning it traps heat far better than thin glass or plastic.

It also will not warp, sag, or yellow in the sun like your acrylic will. If you pull the side panels off a standard fish tank, you have heavy-duty, flat glass that is perfect for greenhouse-style heating.

The Catch: Thermal Shock

The sides of standard aquariums are almost always made from annealed (plate) glass, not tempered glass. Aquariums use annealed glass because it can bow and flex slightly under the immense pressure of the water. If they used tempered glass, that same flexing pressure would cause the entire pane to explode.

Because it is not tempered, aquarium glass is highly susceptible to thermal shock.

When your solar box is baking in the sun at 180°F, the glass is expanded. If a sudden, cool rain shower hits the top of that glass, the top surface rapidly cools and shrinks while the bottom surface is still hot and expanded. That stress will cause the glass to crack instantly.

Worse, when annealed glass cracks, it breaks into large, heavy, razor-sharp shards that would drop straight down into your melted wax and sieve layers.

The Verdict

Yes, aquarium glass will work exceptionally well for your prototype, and it will trap heat much better than what you are currently using.

You just have to treat it carefully. Do not drop cold water on it while it is operating, and if a summer thunderstorm rolls in, you need to throw a tarp over the box or move it into the garage before the rain hits the hot glass.

turns.prompt_text: I'd like to know how to orient the box, but also what if I wrapped it with something, some kind of insulation?
turns.response_html:
Wrapping the box in insulation is exactly how you stop conduction loss through the wood, and getting the angle right ensures you are catching the maximum amount of radiation to begin with. Here is how to dial in both.

The Optimal Angle

To get the most heat, the sun's rays need to hit your glass at exactly a 90-degree (perpendicular) angle. If the angle is too shallow, the light reflects off the glass instead of passing through it.

Because the sun's path changes throughout the year, the ideal tilt of your box depends entirely on your latitude and the season.

At your latitude in central Iowa (around 42° N), the summer sun is very high in the sky. To catch it perfectly during these peak summer months, you want to point the glass True South, and tilt the box back to an angle of roughly 25 to 27 degrees off the flat ground (the general rule for summer is your latitude minus 15 degrees).

If you plan to use it in the fall when the sun sits lower in the sky, you would actually want a much steeper tilt—around 42 degrees (equal to your latitude).
